title: Follow the Flow, Not the Pile

scenes.tts: Autophagy wraps cell material in carriers and sends it to lysosomes for recycling. Those carriers are autophagosomes. Yet two cells can hold the same large pile. Is autophagy faster in both? One makes and clears them quickly. The other makes them slowly, but its exit is blocked. A still picture cannot distinguish those stories.
scenes.visual: Hook on one large cell cross-section filling at least 70 percent of frame height. A blue cup wraps a gray piece of cell material, closes into a double-membrane carrier, and moves toward a large orange recycling compartment. Label the carrier 'autophagosome' and the compartment 'lysosome' only after each appears. Then replay the same map twice using a vertical time scrubber: first, many carriers enter and leave; second, few enter while a red block closes the exit. Freeze both replays on the same final pool size. Keep blue carriers drifting slowly. Label the comparison 'schematic'.

scenes.visual: Keep the cellular recycling map visible and moving faintly. Dim it slightly and place the title 'Follow the Flow, Not the Pile' over the center for 1.8 seconds, then restore full contrast.

scenes.tts: The endoplasmic reticulum, or E R, uses helpers to retry proteins that have not reached their working shape. This is a first picture. In the E R, many failed proteins are returned to the cytosol, tagged with ubiquitin, and destroyed by the proteasome. Ubiquitin is that small protein tag. The proteasome is a capped barrel that unfolds and destroys tagged individual proteins.

scenes.visual: Zoom into the left side of the same cell. A large gray ER lumen occupies most of the frame. A simple gray squiggle labelled 'client' enters. Two teal helper blocks hold it, release it, and hold it again along one looped arrow labelled 'first picture'. On persistent failure, return the client across the ER boundary, add a small red 'ubiquitin' tag, and move it toward a gold barrel labelled 'proteasome'. Animate the squiggle straightening and threading through the barrel. No molecular structures.

scenes.tts: Now a damaged mitochondrion reaches the same station. It cannot enter the proteasome's narrow barrel. Macroautophagy uses a different physical solution. A blue membrane cup grows around the cargo and closes into an autophagosome. In macroautophagy, autophagosomes carry bulk cytoplasm and whole organelles to lysosomes. The carrier fuses with a lysosome, whose acidic interior digests the cargo into reusable blocks.
scenes.visual: Zoom back to the full recycling map. Carry the gold proteasome to the upper right for continuity. Bring in one large gray mitochondrion cartoon, clearly too wide for the proteasome entrance. Grow two blue arcs around it until they close as a double membrane. Move this autophagosome to a large orange lysosome, merge the outer boundary, and transform the inner membrane and mitochondrion into six small gray building-block squares.

scenes.tts: Starvation reduces building blocks arriving from outside the cell, so the reuse bin begins to empty. More cytoplasm now enters autophagosomes and reaches lysosomes. Digestion sends recovered blocks back into the bin. During starvation, autophagy recycles cell material into reusable building blocks. That recycling may be one reason autophagy-defective yeast lose viability faster during nitrogen starvation.
scenes.visual: Keep the same full-cell map. Show an external inlet feeding a central reuse bin, then narrow that inlet under a large 'starvation' label. Let the bin's level fall. Increase blue carrier movement toward the orange lysosome. Send the resulting gray blocks back into the reuse bin until its level partially recovers. Mark the sequence 'schematic'. End with a small yeast-cell silhouette beside the map, one normal and one with the autophagy route crossed out.

scenes.tts: Now watch the carrier pool between its two gates. For a defined cellular pool, change equals arrival minus clearance over the interval. Matching rates keep the pool level. Faster arrival makes it grow. Slower clearance does too. For a defined cellular pool, a larger pool can mean faster arrival or slower clearance. We need an experiment that separates those possibilities.
scenes.visual: Center the blue carrier pool between a left arrow labelled 'arrival' and a right arrow labelled 'clearance'. Use moving dots to show equal rates while a vertical pool gauge stays level. Then create the same high gauge by two transformations: thicken the arrival arrow once, reset, then narrow the clearance arrow. Keep an on-screen equation in plain text: 'pool change = arrival − clearance'. Label all rates and gauge traces 'schematic'.

We need an experiment that separates those possibilities.

scenes.tts: L C three two is a protein form attached to autophagosome membranes, so it marks the carriers. Bafilomycin blocks lysosomal acidification, closing the exit during this short assay. Now two L C three two pools start equally high. After bafilomycin, which pool rises more: the one with fast arrival or slow arrival?

scenes.visual: Split the carried recycling map into two synchronized copies. Place purple LC3-II marks on each blue autophagosome membrane, then label them 'LC3-II'. Both copies begin with the same high carrier pool. The left copy has a thick blue arrival arrow labelled 'fast arrival'; the right has a thin arrow labelled 'slow arrival'. Add the same red bafilomycin block across both orange lysosomal exits. Put the question across the top and 'schematic' below each pool. Purple marks continue subtle ambient drift.

scenes.visual: Hold the predict frame and question for 4.5 seconds. Keep only subtle purple-dot drift inside each pool; do not reveal either result.

scenes.tts: The fast-arrival pool rises more after clearance stops. Its purple gauge climbs steeply while the slow-arrival gauge barely moves. Under a complete lysosomal block that leaves carrier formation unchanged, the extra L C three two estimates lysosomal turnover over the interval. The equal starting amounts could not reveal that difference.

scenes.visual: Advance both schematic gauges for the same displayed time interval. Make the left purple gauge rise steeply and the right rise slightly. Highlight each increment in yellow and label it 'extra accumulation'. Keep both starting levels aligned with a dashed line. Add a small condition below the gauges: 'formation unchanged'. Do not show the lesson's Control, Starved, or Drug D numbers.

scenes.tts: Return to the two cells with equal carrier piles. Their visible amounts matched, but their flows did not. Closing the exit exposed the difference in arrival. The same question works across the recycling map, even when the cargo and route change. Wherever material piles up, ask two questions. How fast does it arrive? How fast does it leave?
scenes.visual: Reassemble the two synchronized cells from the prediction, keeping their equal starting levels marked. Replay the block and let the fast-arrival pool climb farther. Then merge them into the single full-cell recycling map without adding new objects. Run the established ER-to-proteasome and autophagosome-to-lysosome motions quietly while highlighting the left arrival gate followed by the right clearance gate.

scenes.visual: Fade the map to a dark outline while its arrival and clearance arrows continue one slow pulse. Center the end-card line in large white text: 'Follow the flow, not the pile.'
